consumer_dispositions.current_statement_or_definition:
Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $q\ge1$ and $n\ge1$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ and $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_q):\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^q$ be measurable with $\int|f|\,dP<\infty$ and $\int|h_j|\,dP<\infty$ for every $j$; these are integrals in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. For any integrable $g$ write $Pg:=\int_{\mathsf X}g\,dP$. Write $\mu=Pf$ and $\theta=Ph\in\mathbb R^q$, where $\theta$ is known, and use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] for variance and covariance. Given an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and a fixed coefficient $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the **control-variate estimator** is

$$
\widehat\mu_\beta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\bigr].
$$

For one scalar control this is $n^{-1}\sum_i[f(X_i)-\beta(h(X_i)-\theta)]$. The coefficient is fixed independently of the production sample in this definition; a coefficient fitted from that same sample is treated separately.

Let $n\ge1$, assume $P f^2<\infty$ and $P h_j^2<\infty$ for each component, and set $\mu=Pf$, $\theta=Ph$. Define the vector covariance matrix and cross-covariance vector by $\Sigma_{jk}=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(h_k-\theta_k)]$ and $c_j=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(f-\mu)]$. A matrix $\Sigma$ is positive definite when $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero $v$. For an IID sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$ and a fixed $\beta\in\mathbb R^q$, the estimator in [[def-control-variate-estimator]] is unbiased and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_\beta)=\frac1n\operatorname{Var}_P\bigl(f-\beta^{\mathsf T}h\bigr).
$$

If $\Sigma$ is positive definite, the unique variance-minimizing vector coefficient and the minimum variance are

$$
\beta^*=\Sigma^{-1}c,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\beta^*})=\frac1n\left(\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}c\right).
$$

For a scalar control with $\operatorname{Var}_P(h)>0$, this reads $\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}_P(f,h)/\operatorname{Var}_P(h)$. If controls are redundant, delete redundant directions or use the theorem only on a positive-definite covariance subspace; no inverse is asserted for a singular $\Sigma$.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For $Z_i=f(X_i)-\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)$, the expectation convention [F6] and linearity [F3] give $E Z_i=Pf-\beta^{\mathsf T}(Ph-\theta)=\mu$. Thus $E\widehat\mu_\beta=\mu$. [F1, F3, F6]

1.2 The $Z_i$ are the same measurable function of the IID variables $X_i$, so [F2] and [F4] make them IID. [F2, F4]

1.3 By [F7]–[F8], the variance as a function of $\beta$ is $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-2\beta^{\mathsf T}c+\beta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\beta$. [F7, F8]

2.1 Expanding the centered square of $n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i$, the diagonal terms contribute $n^{-2}n\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)$. For $i\ne j$, $Z_i-EZ_i$ and $Z_j-EZ_j$ are independent integrable variables, so [F5] factors their product expectation into zero. Hence $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_\beta)=n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}(Z_1)=n^{-1}\operatorname{Var}_P(f-\beta^{\mathsf T}h)$. [F5, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If $\Sigma$ is positive definite, substituting $c=\Sigma\beta^*$ and completing the square gives $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)-c^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}c+(\beta-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(\beta-\beta^*)$. The last term is nonnegative and vanishes only at $\beta=\beta^*$; for $q=1$ the displayed scalar formula follows. [step 1.3, algebra] ∎

Let $d,n\ge1$, let $\mathsf X$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathsf X$, and let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Let $U_i=(U_{i1},\ldots,U_{id})$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, be IID random vectors whose coordinates are mutually independent and each have the uniform law on $[0,1]$, meaning $P(U_{ij}\le t)=t$ for $0\le t\le1$. Let $T:[0,1]^d\to\mathsf X$ be measurable and satisfy $T(U_1)\sim P$. Define the reflected input $1-U_i=(1-U_{i1},\ldots,1-U_{id})$ and the antithetic estimator by

$$
\widehat\mu_{\rm anti}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{f(T(U_i))+f(T(1-U_i))}{2}.
$$

The two outputs in each pair may be dependent; pairs with different indices are independent. The variance comparison in the theorem uses $2n$ function evaluations and compares with an ordinary mean of $2n$ independent $P$-draws. IID and mutual independence have the meanings of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and variance/covariance use [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

consumer_dispositions.current_statement_or_definition: Let $d\ge1$, let $U_1,\ldots,U_d$ be independent real random variables, and let $G,H:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel functions with $E[G(U)^2]<\infty$ and $E[H(U)^2]<\infty$. A function is nondecreasing in coordinate $j$ when increasing only its $j$th input cannot decrease its value; nonincreasing is defined with the reverse inequality. Suppose $G$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate and $H$ is nonincreasing in each coordinate. Then $\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))\le0$.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 In dimension one, let $\mu$ be the law of $U_1$. Expanding the double integral and applying [F3] gives $2\operatorname{Cov}(G(U_1),H(U_1))=\int\!\int (G(x)-G(y))(H(x)-H(y))\,\mu(dx)\mu(dy)$. The integrand is nonpositive for every $x,y$ because the two functions have opposite monotonicity, so the covariance is nonpositive. The products are integrable by square-integrability and [F4]. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Assume the claim holds for $d-1$ and first suppose $G,H$ are bounded. By [F2] the joint law is $\mu\times\nu$, where $\mu$ is the first $d-1$ coordinate laws and $\nu$ is the law of $U_d$. Define $G_0(x)=\int G(x,z)\,\nu(dz)$ and $H_0(x)=\int H(x,z)\,\nu(dz)$. Fubini [F3] makes these measurable and bounded; they retain their respective coordinate monotonicities. For each fixed $x$, step 1.1 applied to the last coordinate gives $\operatorname{Cov}_\nu(G(x,U_d),H(x,U_d))\le0$, and the induction hypothesis gives $\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(G_0,H_0)\le0$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 Expanding both sides by the covariance formula [F5] and integrating with [F3] yields $\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))=\int \operatorname{Cov}_\nu(G(x,U_d),H(x,U_d))\,\mu(dx)+\operatorname{Cov}_\mu(G_0,H_0)\le0$. Thus the bounded case holds in dimension $d$, completing the induction. [F3, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For general square-integrable $G,H$, clamp each function to $[-m,m]$. The clamps remain coordinatewise monotone and bounded, and $|G_m-G|^2\le G^2$, $|H_m-H|^2\le H^2$. Applying [F6] to these squared differences gives $L^2$ convergence. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and the covariance identity [F5] then imply $\operatorname{Cov}(G_m(U),H_m(U))\to\operatorname{Cov}(G(U),H(U))$. Each bounded covariance is nonpositive by step 3.1, so the limit is nonpositive. [F4, F5, F6, step 3.1] ∎

consumer_dispositions.current_statement_or_definition:
Use the setup of [[def-antithetic-randomized-sampling]], assume $E_P[f^2]<\infty$, and put $Y=f(T(U_1))$, $\widetilde Y=f(T(1-U_1))$, $\mu=E_Pf$, and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_P(f)$. Then $Y$ and $\widetilde Y$ have the same law and mean, and the antithetic estimator from $n$ independent input pairs is unbiased with

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm anti})=\frac{\sigma^2+\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)}{2n}.
$$

Compared with the ordinary mean of $2n$ independent draws from $P$, whose variance is $\sigma^2/(2n)$, antithetic sampling has no larger variance exactly when $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)\le0$, and has strictly smaller variance exactly when this covariance is negative. A sufficient condition is that $g=f\circ T$ is coordinatewise monotone on $[0,1]^d$ (each coordinate may have either monotonicity direction). In particular, when $\mathsf X$ is a subset of $\mathbb R^m$ with the order $x\le y$ defined by $x_j\le y_j$ for every coordinate, if $T$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing as a map into $\mathsf X$ and $f$ is nondecreasing for that order, then $g$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For a uniform coordinate, $P(U_{1j}=s)=0$ for every $s\in[0,1]$, since $P(U_{1j}\le s)=s$ and the left limit of this cdf at $s$ is also $s$. Thus for $0\le t\le1$, $P(1-U_{1j}\le t)=P(U_{1j}\ge1-t)=1-P(U_{1j}<1-t)=t$. By [F3], the reflected coordinates remain independent; [F4] then shows $1-U_1$ has the same product-uniform law as $U_1$. Since $T$ and $f$ are measurable, $Y$ and $\widetilde Y$ have the same law, mean $\mu$, and variance $\sigma^2$. [F1, F3, F4]

1.2 The pair value $Z_i=[f(T(U_i))+f(T(1-U_i))]/2$ is a measurable function of $U_i$. Thus the $Z_i$ are IID by [F2]–[F3], each has mean $\mu$ by [F9], and their average is unbiased. [F1, F2, F3, F9]

2.1 By [F5]–[F6], $\operatorname{Var}(Z_i)=[\operatorname{Var}(Y)+\operatorname{Var}(\widetilde Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)]/4=[\sigma^2+\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)]/2$. For distinct $i,j$, the centered $Z_i,Z_j$ are independent, so [F7] gives zero covariance; expanding the centered square of their average therefore gives the stated variance divided by $n$. [F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The mean of $2n$ independent $P$-draws has variance $\sigma^2/(2n)$ by the same centered-square expansion and [F7]. Comparing this with step 2.1 gives the iff conditions for weak and strict variance reduction. [F5, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $g=f\circ T$ is coordinatewise nondecreasing, then $g(1-u)$ is coordinatewise nonincreasing, so [F8] gives $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,\widetilde Y)\le0$. More generally, if the monotonicity direction varies by coordinate, define $S_j(v)=v_j$ in increasing coordinates and $S_j(v)=1-v_j$ in decreasing coordinates. Then $V=S(U_1)$ is still product-uniform, $\phi=g\circ S$ is nondecreasing in all coordinates, and $S(1-v)=1-S(v)$ coordinatewise. Consequently $g(U_1)=\phi(V)$ and $g(1-U_1)=\phi(1-V)$, so [F8] applies. In the stated ordered-subset case, $u\le v$ coordinatewise implies $T(u)\le T(v)$ and then $f(T(u))\le f(T(v))$, which proves the advertised monotonicity of $g$. [F1, F3, F4, F8, step 1.1, given] ∎

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,P)$ be a probability space, let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable, and let $H\ge1$ and $A_1,\ldots,A_H$ be a finite measurable partition of $\mathsf X$ with $p_h=P(A_h)>0$. Define the conditional stratum law by $P_h(B)=P(B\cap A_h)/p_h$ for $B\in\mathcal X$. Choose fixed integers $n_h\ge1$ and put $n=\sum_{h=1}^H n_h$. Draw mutually independent variables $X_{hj}$, with $X_{h1},\ldots,X_{hn_h}$ IID under $P_h$ as in [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]], and define $\bar f_h=n_h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_h}f(X_{hj})$. Expectations and variances use [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]] and [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The **stratified Monte Carlo estimator** of $Pf$ is

$$
\widehat\mu_{\rm strat}=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h\bar f_h.
$$

The allocation $(n_1,\ldots,n_H)$ is part of the design. A variance comparison must specify it and the comparator.

Use the setup of [[def-stratified-monte-carlo-estimator]] and suppose $\int_{\mathsf X} f^2\,dP<\infty$. Write $\mu=\int_{\mathsf X}f\,dP$, $\mu_h=E_{P_h}f$, and $\sigma_h^2=\operatorname{Var}_{P_h}(f)$. The estimator is unbiased and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm strat})=\sum_{h=1}^H\frac{p_h^2\sigma_h^2}{n_h}.
$$

If, additionally, each $np_h$ is a positive integer and the fixed allocation is proportional, $n_h=np_h$, then the variance is no larger than that of the ordinary IID sample mean of the same total size $n$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\rm strat})=\frac1n\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}_P(f)}n.
$$

The comparison is only asserted for this proportional allocation; a general fixed allocation has the variance in the first display and need not beat the IID comparator.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For each $h$, [F1] gives $\int_{\mathsf X}f^2\,dP_h=p_h^{-1}\int_{A_h}f^2\,dP<\infty$. Since $|f|\le1+f^2$, $f$ is integrable under $P$ and every $P_h$. Thus [F3] gives $\mu_h=p_h^{-1}\int_{A_h}f\,dP$, and [F4] plus the finite partition identity yield $E\widehat\mu_{\rm strat}=\sum_h p_h\mu_h=\sum_h\int_{A_h}f\,dP=\int f\,dP=\mu$. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 For fixed $h$, expand the centered square of $\bar f_h$. The diagonal terms give $\sigma_h^2/n_h$; for distinct draws the centered product expectation is zero by independence and [F5]. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(\bar f_h)=\sigma_h^2/n_h$. [F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Splitting $\int(f-\mu)^2dP$ over the partition and writing $f-\mu=(f-\mu_h)+(\mu_h-\mu)$ on $A_h$, the cross term integrates to zero since $\int_{A_h}(f-\mu_h)dP=p_hE_{P_h}(f-\mu_h)=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)=\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2+\sum_h p_h(\mu_h-\mu)^2$. [F1, F3, F4, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1] and [F7], the sigma-algebras generated by all individual draws are independent. Grouping them by stratum and applying [F8] shows that the sigma-algebras generated by the disjoint stratum blocks are independent. Each $\bar f_h$ is measurable with respect to its block sigma-algebra because it is a finite sum of measurable values of $f$, using [F9]; hence the stratum averages are independent. Applying [F5] to their centered products and expanding the variance of $\sum_h p_h\bar f_h$ gives $\sum_h p_h^2\sigma_h^2/n_h$. [F1, F5, F7, F8, F9, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Under $n_h=np_h$, step 3.1 becomes $n^{-1}\sum_h p_h\sigma_h^2$. The ordinary mean of $n$ IID $P$-draws has variance $\operatorname{Var}_P(f)/n$, by the same centered-square expansion as step 2.1. Step 2.2 shows the difference is $n^{-1}\sum_h p_h(\mu_h-\mu)^2\ge0$, proving the comparison. [F2, F5, F6, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

Use the notation $Pg=\int g\,dP$ from [[def-control-variate-estimator]]. Let $n\ge1$, let $q\ge1$ be fixed, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P$, and assume $P|f|^4<\infty$ and $P|h_j|^4<\infty$ for each $j$. Set $\theta=Ph$, define $\Sigma_{jk}=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(h_k-\theta_k)]$ and $c_j=E_P[(h_j-\theta_j)(f-Pf)]$, and suppose $\Sigma$ is positive definite, meaning $v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v>0$ for every nonzero vector $v$. Put $\beta^*=\Sigma^{-1}c$. Define $\bar f_n=n^{-1}\sum_i f(X_i)$, $\bar h_n=n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)$,

$$\widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_i(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \widehat c_n=\frac1n\sum_i(h(X_i)-\bar h_n)(f(X_i)-\bar f_n).$$

and let $\widehat\beta_n=\widehat\Sigma_n^{-1}\widehat c_n$ when $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is invertible and $0$ otherwise. For a scalar random sequence $R_n$, write $R_n=O_P(n^{-1})$ when $nR_n$ is bounded in probability: for each $\varepsilon>0$ some finite $M$ and $N$ satisfy $P(|nR_n|>M)<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$. For a fixed-dimensional vector or matrix, $O_P(a_n)$ means its Euclidean or Frobenius norm divided by $a_n$ is bounded in probability. Then

$$\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta_n}-\widehat\mu_{\beta^*}=-(\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)=O_P(n^{-1}).$$

This result bounds only the same-sample coefficient-times-control-mean remainder; it does not assert that $\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta_n}$ is unbiased.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The entries $h_j(X_i)$, $f(X_i)$, $h_j(X_i)h_k(X_i)$, and $h_j(X_i)f(X_i)$ are measurable by [F11]. Since each $X_i$ has law $P$, applying the same measurable function to each gives a common law; [F10] preserves their mutual independence, so each resulting sequence is IID by [F2]. The fourth-moment hypothesis and [F8] make every product entry integrable, and [F9] identifies its expectation with the corresponding integral under $P$. Applying [F4] to these IID sequences gives $\bar h_n\to\theta$, $\bar f_n\to Pf$, $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)h(X_i)^{\mathsf T}\to E_P[hh^{\mathsf T}]$, and $n^{-1}\sum_i h(X_i)f(X_i)\to E_P[hf]$ almost surely. The centered formulas therefore give $\widehat\Sigma_n\to\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n\to c$ almost surely; positive definiteness of $\Sigma$ and continuity of determinant imply $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is eventually invertible almost surely. The fallback definition makes $\widehat\beta_n$ measurable: on the open nonsingular set the inverse entries are ratios of polynomial functions, and on its closed complement the value is constant. [F2, F3, F4, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, algebra]

2.1 Each scalar entry of $h$, $f$, $hh^{\mathsf T}$, and $hf$ has finite variance: for products, [F8] gives $E[h_j^2h_k^2]\le(Eh_j^4Eh_k^4)^{1/2}$ and $E[h_j^2f^2]\le(Eh_j^4Ef^4)^{1/2}$. Independence and [F6] make distinct centered sample entries have zero covariance, so each raw sample average has variance its population variance divided by $n$. With $a=M/\sqrt n$, [F5] bounds each entry's deviation probability by its variance divided by $M^2/n$; choosing $M$ large proves the $O_P(n^{-1/2})$ rates. Fixed $q$ makes the finite union of entrywise bounds joint. Centering changes the raw moments by products of sample-mean errors, which are $O_P(n^{-1})$; hence $\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma$ and $\widehat c_n-c$ are jointly $O_P(n^{-1/2})$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1]

3.1 On the event that $\widehat\Sigma_n$ is invertible, $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=\widehat\Sigma_n^{-1}[(\widehat c_n-c)-(\widehat\Sigma_n-\Sigma)\beta^*]$, since $c=\Sigma\beta^*$. Step 1.1 and the adjugate-over-determinant formula show that the inverse converges to $\Sigma^{-1}$ almost surely on the eventually nonsingular set; extending it by zero on the singular event gives an $O_P(1)$ matrix sequence. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose bounds for this inverse norm and for the bracket in step 2.1 after scaling by $\sqrt n$, with total failure probability less than $\varepsilon/2$. On their intersection the product is bounded after scaling by $\sqrt n$, so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*=O_P(n^{-1/2})$ there. The singular-event probability tends to zero by step 1.1; the fallback value $0$ therefore does not change this order in probability. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], subtracting the two estimators cancels $\bar f_n$ and leaves exactly $-(\widehat\beta_n-\beta^*)^{\mathsf T}(\bar h_n-\theta)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose finite bounds for each factor after scaling by $\sqrt n$ so that the probability either bound fails is less than $\varepsilon/2$; on their intersection, Cauchy--Schwarz in $\mathbb R^q$ bounds $n$ times the absolute inner product by the product of those bounds. Thus the inner product is $O_P(n^{-1})$ by definition. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Let $n,q\ge1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P$, let $f,h_1,\ldots,h_q$ be integrable, and let $\theta=E_P h$ be known. Write $\mathcal X_n$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the production sample, namely the smallest sigma-algebra containing each event $\{X_i\in B\}$ for measurable $B$. Let $\mathcal P$ be a sigma-algebra generated by pilot data and assume $\mathcal P$ and $\mathcal X_n$ are independent in the sense of [[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]]. Let the $\mathcal P$-measurable coefficient $\widehat\beta\in\mathbb R^q$ satisfy $E\|\widehat\beta\|<\infty$. Then the random-coefficient control estimator

$$
\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}=\frac1n\sum_i\left[f(X_i)-\widehat\beta^{\mathsf T}(h(X_i)-\theta)\right]
$$

is integrable and $E[\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}\mid\mathcal P]=E_Pf$ almost surely. The first-moment condition on $\widehat\beta$ ensures the displayed estimator is integrable; no claim is made for an arbitrary nonintegrable pilot coefficient.
consumer_dispositions.current_argument:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The production sample means are $\mathcal X_n$-measurable and satisfy $E\bar f=E_Pf$ and $E(\bar h-\theta)=0$ by [F2], [F5], and [F6]. Each $\widehat\beta_j$ is $\mathcal P$-measurable; for any Borel sets, its preimage event belongs to $\mathcal P$ while the corresponding production-mean event belongs to $\mathcal X_n$, so [F7] makes it independent of each production mean. Since $E\|\widehat\beta\|<\infty$, [F4] applied to the absolute product makes every $\widehat\beta_j(\bar h_j-\theta_j)$ integrable; the full estimator is therefore integrable. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7]

2.1 Let $A\in\mathcal P$. The random variable $\bar f$ is $\mathcal X_n$-measurable, so its Borel preimage events are independent of $A$ by [F7]; factorization [F4] gives $E[1_A\bar f]=P(A)E_Pf$. Also $1_A\widehat\beta_j$ is $\mathcal P$-measurable and independent of $\bar h_j-\theta_j$, which is $\mathcal X_n$-measurable, so [F4] gives $E[1_A\widehat\beta_j(\bar h_j-\theta_j)]=E[1_A\widehat\beta_j]E(\bar h_j-\theta_j)=0$. By [F1] and [F5], $E[1_A\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}]=P(A)E_Pf$. [F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1]

3.1 The constant $E_Pf$ is $\mathcal P$-measurable and its integral on every $A\in\mathcal P$ equals the integral of the estimator on $A$ by step 2.1. The defining characterization [F3] therefore gives $E[\widehat\mu_{\widehat\beta}\mid\mathcal P]=E_Pf$ almost surely. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

excerpts.Definition:
Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.
excerpts.Remarks: The formula above defines the mathematical sample variance. Computing it as the difference between the sample second moment and the squared sample mean can suffer catastrophic cancellation in floating-point arithmetic; no stable-update or floating-point error bound is asserted on this page.

excerpts.Statement: Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence. If $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$ and $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$, then $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=\mu$ for every $n\ge1$. If also $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, then $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\sigma^2/n$ for every $n\ge1$.
excerpts.Facts & Assumptions:
**Given:** A real IID sequence $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ on one probability space; in the first claim $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, and in the second claim $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$.

[F1] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: IID means that all variables have the same law and the whole family is mutually independent.

[F2] [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]: For a measurable $g$, if $g(X)$ is integrable, then its expectation is the integral of $g$ against the law of $X$.

[F3] [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]: Expectation is linear on integrable real random variables.

[F4] [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]: For square-integrable real $X$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2]$.

[F5] [[cor-variance-adds-for-pairwise-independent-random-variables]]: For a finite pairwise-independent family of square-integrable real random variables, the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances.

[F6] [[def-iid-monte-carlo-estimators]]: $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$.
excerpts.Proof:
1.1 Every $Y_i$ has the law of $Y_1$ by [F1]. Applying [F2] to the identity map gives $\mathbb E[Y_i]=\mu$ when $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$. If $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, applying [F2] to $y\mapsto(y-\mu)^2$ also gives $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sigma^2$ by [F4]. [F1, F2, F4, given]

2.1 By [F6], $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Linearity [F3] and step 1.1 therefore give $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E[Y_i]=\mu$. [F3, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Assume $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$. Since $|y|\le1+y^2$ for every real $y$, each $Y_i$ is integrable as well as square-integrable. The first $n$ terms are pairwise independent by [F1], so [F5] and step 1.1 give $\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^nY_i)=n\sigma^2$. From [F4], scaling the centered sum by $1/n$ multiplies its variance by $1/n^2$; hence $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=n^{-2}(n\sigma^2)=\sigma^2/n$. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎
